answer.rationale: The two memories that actually bear weight on this decision are memory_c2 (the low-cost vendor switch that 'cut unit cost sharply') and memory_c4 (renegotiation recovering real margin at renewal). memory_c2 is the one that would justify the single decision that satisfies the 18% mandate outright, so it deserves scrutiny: the consolidated note records cost and invoicing accuracy but says nothing about on-time delivery, fill rate, or whether that switch happened while the line had buffer. Switching primary supply at 94% of committed volume with zero buffer and 14 days to expiry means any onboarding slip converts directly into missed deliveries — the summary's silence on delivery performance is exactly the gap that could make it misleading here. memory_c4 needs verification for the opposite reason: I intend to rely on it, and I need to know how much price movement benchmarking actually produced, since if it was 4-5% it cannot carry an 18% mandate alone. Given one decision this cycle, negotiating with the incumbent is the only move that pursues the cost target while holding delivery risk flat (memory_c1: integration stable, no migration work), and memory_c6 suggests term length is a real lever on unit price. I scope it as a guarded step — press on price and payment terms without accepting a long multi-year lock-in, and keep the low-cost vendor's quote live as leverage and as a qualified alternate for next review, when add_second_source (memory_c3) can address the single-point-of-failure exposure that this cycle leaves untouched. Downstream risk to flag explicitly: an 18% cut chased in one move can quietly buy cost with reliability, and a multi-year commitment taken for unit price forecloses the second-sourcing option later; if verification shows negotiation historically yielded only single-digit movement, the honest outcome is a partial cut this cycle plus a staged vendor qualification, not a forced full switch. I am not treating either memory as settled until the archive records are read.
